source.title: Fine-tuning large language models for domain adaptation: exploration of training strategies, scaling, model merging and synergistic capabilities
source.authors: Wei Lu; Rachel K. Luu; Markus J. Buehler

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some formatting and typographical errors appear, but the relevant sections are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares downstream benchmark performance across model families with different parameter counts and reported pretraining-token counts. This is a different measure and an uncontrolled comparison, not a test of held-out cross-entropy scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy, fit scaling-law exponents, test extrapolation from smaller runs, or find compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Its token-count and model-family performance comparisons bear on V6 only. Kaplan et al.'s scaling-law result is cited, not tested.
record.test_reason: The study is about fine-tuning and model merging, not scaling. Its only scaling-relevant result is Figure 18. That figure plots downstream domain-benchmark performance of three fine-tuned model families against pretraining-token count (1T, 8T, 15T) and reports a rising trend with diminishing gains. This bears weakly on V6 in a new setting: domain-adapted, fine-tuned models. It is a three-point, uncontrolled, cross-family comparison with no fitted or validated prediction, so T3 fits better than T2. No held-out loss, fits, extrapolation, allocation or shape tests appear.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors describe an approximate trend in which more pretraining tokens give better downstream performance with diminishing relative improvements, and caution that families differ in architecture, training and data. They link this to the consensus of diminishing returns with data and model size. Their headline scale conclusion is different: model merging produces emergent gains only in 7–8B models, not at 1.7B.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates fine-tuned domain models on downstream benchmarks rather than measuring held-out pretraining loss or fitting scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors note that architecture, training strategy, dataset, and prompting differ or may affect results.

fits_no_version.finding: SLERP model merging gives synergistic gains above both parents for 7B and 8B models, but degrades performance for the 1.7B SmolLM (Figures 7C, 12, 13). The authors call this a scale-dependent threshold effect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benefits of weight-space model merging (emergent capabilities) depend on model scale and appear only above a size threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: A larger but noisier CPT corpus lowered Llama performance (Figure 9) and left Mistral nearly unchanged (0.80 vs 0.81).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: More continued-pretraining data does not help downstream performance when data quality falls.

record.problems: The token-count comparison is explicitly approximate and confounded by differences in model architecture, training strategy, and datasets. The study reports downstream benchmark performance rather than held-out cross-entropy, provides no fitted predictive relationship, and reports no uncertainty for these comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results bearing on the tested version were left out. The study's fine-tuning, merging, and conversation results do not test the scaling claim.

untested.parts: No relation to pretraining loss. No fitted or validated prediction of downstream performance. No within-family scaling series.
Entire version: no held-out pretraining loss or power-law fits.
Entire version: no fixed-size shape comparison.

missing.what: GPT-4o-judged intelligence scores from one open-ended conversation. The smallest model (SmolLM 1.7B CPT-SFT-DPO) scored highest: total 38/40, normalized 10.0, above Llama 8B (8.7) and Mistral 7B (7.9, 6.3). This is a downstream measure that does not rise with scale.

record.verdict_notes: Kaplan et al. is cited only to speculate that merging gains scale with parameter count. Figure 18's three points are after domain fine-tuning with different data mixes (SmolLM followed its own Instruct recipe), so pretraining tokens are confounded with family, size and fine-tuning. Both V6 labels rest on very weak evidence.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law fit across parameters, tokens, or compute.
No extrapolation from smaller runs to larger runs.
No fixed-compute comparison or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
No controlled comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No test of the same power-law form in other modalities or training regimes.
The study reports downstream domain-benchmark results, not a predictive relationship with pretraining loss; it does not fit or validate a prediction rule.
No analysis of scaling-law fitting choices, exponents, or departures from a single power law.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1, Mistral, and SmolLM model families (cross-family comparison)
rows.stage_stated: Fine-tuned models; the paper compares families with different pretraining-token counts
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream benchmark performance across model families with different pretraining-token counts.

conditions.value: 1 trillion for SmolLM, 8 trillion for Mistral, and 15 trillion for Llama-3.1
Performance on the study's domain benchmarks; exact values are figure only

rows.measure: Downstream domain-benchmark performance over pretraining-token count
rows.note: The authors describe an approximate overall trend in which more pretraining tends to yield better performance, with diminishing relative improvements. They caution that architectures, training strategies, and datasets differ, so this is not a controlled or predictive scaling test.
rows.check: The direction the authors describe matches V6: more pretraining gives better performance, with diminishing relative gains. However, there are only three points from different families (architecture, data, fine-tuning mix all differ). Values are figure-only and there is no baseline. No predictive rule is fitted, so the 'predictably' part of V6 is not tested.

rows.subject: Llama (8B), Mistral (7B), and SmolLM (1.7B) model families (aggregate comparison)
rows.operation_detail: Compared benchmark performance and relative improvement across model families.

conditions.value: Performance scores and relative improvement over base models; exact values are figure only

rows.measure: Downstream domain-benchmark performance by model family and size
rows.note: The text says fine-tuned models outperform their non-fine-tuned counterparts, Llama has the highest absolute performance, and SmolLM has the greatest relative improvement. The comparison does not isolate model size from architecture, data, or training differences.
rows.check: Figure 17 compares fine-tuned with non-fine-tuned models and relative improvement over each family's own base. That measures fine-tuning gains, not performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss. The absolute ordering (Llama > Mistral > SmolLM) is confounded by family and duplicates r1's evidence. It should not be linked to V6.

relationships.condition: Three fine-tuned model families (SmolLM 1.7B/1T tokens, Mistral 7B/8T, Llama-3.1 8B/15T) on spider-silk and bio-materials multiple-choice benchmarks
relationships.reason: r1: performance rises with pretraining tokens with diminishing gains, per authors. Weak evidence: three confounded cross-family points, figure only.
relationships.display_finding: Performance increased with diminishing returns across three models with more pretraining tokens, although model family and size also varied.

relationships.condition: Open-ended single-conversation materials-design task scored by GPT-4o (Table 3)
relationships.reason: Based on the text, not the rows: the 1.7B SmolLM variant scored highest (normalized 10.0 vs 8.7 for best Llama 8B). A single conversation, judged by an LLM, so very weak.
relationships.display_finding: SmolLM 1.7B received the highest normalized score, 10.0 versus 8.7 for the best Llama 8B, in a single conversation judged by GPT-4o.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Cross-family downstream domain benchmarks at the reported model sizes and pretraining-token counts
reader_labels.reason: The authors report an approximate trend toward better performance with more pretraining, but note diminishing relative gains and non-comparable architectures, datasets, and training strategies; the results do not establish predictable performance scaling. Rows r1 and r2.
